title: Leno: Bad Car Movies I’ve Loved

body_markdown:
Here at the garage, we used to do bad-car-movie nights in which we’d show *The Car* with James Brolin or *Hot Rods to Hell* or terrible films like that. Fact is, there are far more bad car movies to choose from than good ones. I guess my favorite is *Grand Prix* —it’s a great car movie, and when you remember they did it with cameras the size of suitcases strapped to Formula 1 cars, it’s even more amazing. But for the most part, cars are misunderstood or badly depicted in film. Even Steve McQueen’s *Le Mans* , which we all love, isn’t a great movie. There is nothing funnier than trying to get your wife to watch it. “They’re just driving in a circle! What’s going on!?” They’re furious because there’s no plot to it at all.


*Welcome to the[Hagerty Movies and Cars Celebration](https://www.hagerty.com/media/magazine-features/welcome-to-the-hagerty-movies-and-cars-celebration/) , where we highlight and explore the relationship between[cars and the silver screen](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/movies-and-cars/) .*


Maybe my favorite bad racing movie is *Driven* , the Sly Stallone movie from 2001. First of all, someone gets the keys to the race car, as if race cars have keys. And then they’re racing on the streets of Chicago, like a race car would last five minutes on regular streets, and women’s dresses are blowing up and they go by a cop who’s got the radar going and it reads 195. It’s just so stupid. It reminded me of the Elvis movie *Spinout* , where he’s racing a Cobra and it goes into a lake and comes out a Triumph TR3. Then there’s *Goldfinger* , where he’s driving a brand-new Aston Martin DB5 and he can’t outrun a Mercedes 220 full of Koreans.


Part of the problem is that the people who make movies either don’t know anything about cars or don’t care. Back in 1989, I did a terrible movie called *Collision Course* , and I had big arguments with the director. The movie is about this magic Japanese turbocharger that gets stolen, and the late, great Pat Morita plays a Japanese detective who comes looking for it while I play his partner on the Detroit police force. There’s this chase scene, and the director said, “OK, you pull over, open the hood, put the turbocharger on, and then take off.” I argued that you can’t put a turbocharger on like that and he said, “Just do it!” I guess he thought you can simply lay a turbo on the air cleaner and it works.


I remember they called me to read for another movie, and my line was, “Hey, what kind of magic carpet ride you guys taking out tonight?” I said to the director, “You know, I don’t know any car guy who would talk like that.” Then there was that Jimmy Fallon and Queen Latifah movie, *Taxi* , where she pushes a button and a supercharger rises out of the hood. How does that work?? Even the great Martin Scorsese gets it wrong: In *The Irishman* , Robert De Niro plays a truck driver who has broken down, and Joe Pesci comes up, takes a look, fiddles with a wire, and says, “Timing chain, there’s a cap on it. This cap is loose and it ain’t supposed to be loose, so they get worn out.” Oh, OK.


I think my biggest disappointment was *Ferrari* . Michael Mann is an amazing director, but OK, Ferrari is a guy and he’s cheating on his wife and I don’t care, can we please get back to the cars? It’s a fabulous movie—I just didn’t care about his personal relationships. It’s funny because I think that’s where women and men split on *Ford v Ferrari* , which is an excellent film and actually made money, which is kind of unusual for a car flick. The women I talked to didn’t like it because there’s no love interest in the story and it’s only about cars and racing, and the men liked it because there’s no love interest in the story and it’s only about cars and racing. Oh well, everyone’s a critic.
